title: Schedule
text:
How to read it
Each bar sits on the activity’s early schedule: the earliest it can start given its planned start, today’s date, and the finish of everything it depends on. The solid part of a bar is the reported progress, the hatched tint is what remains. A diamond is an official due date; the faint band behind a bar is the late window, the latest the activity could run without moving a deadline. The 3-pixel edge in the label gutter is the float verdict: red for zero (29 of the 43 open activities today), amber for one to three days.
The lane at the top is everything else the course asks for in the same weeks: squares are homework, triangles quizzes, the black diamond is the final exam, the blue dots are the project deliverables. Weeks 9 to 13 are where the lane and the bars pile up together.

title: Schedule
text:
The rules behind the numbers

Time is counted in calendar days because the team works weekends. An activity occupies its start and due dates inclusive; the duration is the number of days between them.
depends_on in data/activities.csv holds finish-to-start predecessors: an activity cannot start until every predecessor has finished. Planned start dates are start-no-earlier-than constraints; they encode when the course teaches what an activity needs (surveydown arrives Sep 30, cbc_design on Oct 7, mixed logit on Nov 18).
Official due dates are hard finish-no-later-than constraints on the submission activities. The backward pass runs from those, so float is measured against the professor’s deadlines, not against a made-up project end.
Today is the status date. A not-started activity whose planned start has passed is pushed to today; an in-progress one is assumed to finish on its due date or today, whichever is later. Done activities keep their actual dates and carry no float.
Total float is the number of days an activity can slip without moving a deadline. Zero float is the critical chain; one to three days is near-critical. Activities with no deadline downstream (the meeting sign-ups, the ongoing habits) are shown as open-ended rather than given a meaningless number.

The Prolific fielding window (FS04) is assumed to be Nov 17 to Nov 27. The professor launches it; the date should be confirmed at the Nov 11 class. Every day it starts late comes straight out of the final analysis, which has zero float.
The proposal workshop meeting (P05) is booked through the professor’s scheduling link this week; if the slot lands on Friday, the revision (P06) and the move into the official repo (P07) compress into the weekend.
Classmates take the pilot over Oct 21 to 24 (PA01). The feedback sheet is due with HW8 on Oct 26, but the responses to our survey arrive earlier and cleaning starts on the partial data.

title: Week by week
text:
Reading the cadence
Quizzes fall in weeks 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13 and each covers only the material since the previous one; the lowest of six is dropped. Project deliverables land roughly every two to three weeks from week 3 onward, and the heaviest stretch is weeks 9 to 13, when the pilot analysis, final survey and final report overlap with HW8 to HW12 and three quizzes. Week 14 is Thanksgiving with no class but the final survey in the field, so the final analysis cannot start until the data lands; that is the tightest link in the critical path.

section: R and Quarto habits from the course
text:
R and Quarto habits from the course

Open folders, not files: Positron sets the working directory to the opened folder, so relative paths work. On this site _quarto.yml also sets execute-dir: project, so every page reads data with file.path("data", "file.csv") from the repo root.
Paths with file.path(), relative to the opened folder. Never change the working directory from code, never absolute paths, never here() in student files.
No .Rproj files; the course templates ship them and the instruction is to ignore them.
Every report renders cleanly before it is committed; a .qmd that does not render is not submitted.
Charts: informative titles that state the finding, real axis labels, a source caption, white background, direct labels where possible (the my-chart-style skill from week 2 encodes this).
Ask the agent for code, not answers; keep the data, script, figure pipeline; sanity-check row counts, duplicates, NA handling and totals yourself.

title: Conventions

Commit messages say what changed and why (“Add pilot power analysis”, not “update”). Pull before push when someone else may have pushed. Never force-push, never rewrite main. Nothing personal and no credentials in this repo: it is public.

title: The course
section: The loop the course runs on
text:
The loop the course runs on
Prompt, read the diff, verify, commit and push. The agent almost never makes a syntax mistake, so a wrong answer arrives looking exactly like a right one; running is not the same as right. The three habits the course teaches for working safely: ask for code rather than results, run sanity checks the agent cannot fake (row counts, duplicates, spot checks against the source, NA handling, totals that make sense), and use fake data with the same columns when the real data cannot be shared.

title: Context bank
text: The context bank is the standing knowledge behind the tracker: what the course is, when everything is due, what each deliverable must contain and how it is scored, who is on the team and who owns which account, and the conventions the professor grades on. text:
Topic
Smart Urban Living (chosen with the proposal draft of Sep 15): consumer preferences and willingness to pay for smart apartment features. The product is a Smart Urban Apartment Package, a configurable set of smart-home technologies and technology-enabled amenities for modern multifamily rentals, and the study is a choice-based conjoint among U.S. renters.
Against the seven selection criteria, the weak spot is “emerging and pre-commercial”: smart locks and thermostats are common in new Class A buildings. The argument the proposal makes is that the design decision is unresolved for mid-market and retrofit stock, and that no public source gives tradeoff-based willingness to pay per feature, only stated-preference percentages.

title: Critical path
text:
Where the risk concentrates
Three places have no give at all. This week: the proposal workshop, the revision and the move into the official repo all sit between today and Sunday with zero float, because the meeting and the deadline share the week. Weeks 9 to 11: the pilot exchange on Oct 21 feeds a Nov 1 report through a chain of two-day tasks, and the final survey has to be rebuilt and redeployed by Nov 15 with one day of float, while HW8 to HW10 and Quiz 5 land in the same fortnight. Thanksgiving to Dec 6: the Prolific data arrives at the end of the assumed fielding window and the final report is due the Sunday after the in-class exam, so cleaning, modelling, analysis and writing each get about two days.
The defences are already in the plan: start cleaning on partial pilot data (PA02) while the feedback is triaged in parallel (PA05); scaffold every final-analysis script and the report skeleton on the pilot data in the second week of November (FA01, six days of float, so it can absorb a slip without hurting anything); confirm the Prolific launch date at the Nov 11 class so FS04 stops being an assumption.
